 The Tax Brackets Didn’t Expire After All. Does a 67-Year-Old With $1.7 Million Still Need to Rush Roth Conversions?
 Jake FitzGerald Fri, November 13, 2026 at 2:12 AM PST 6 min read Quick Read 
 The One Big Beautiful Bill kept today's brackets, killing the rate-hike deadline, but RMDs, surviving-spouse filing, and heirs still make Roth conversions worth weighing. 
 Filling the 22% bracket for six years costs about $221,000 in tax but shrinks the first RMD from roughly $86,000 to $19,000. 
 A surviving spouse filing single would see the same RMD taxed at 22% instead of 12%, with a far lower Medicare surcharge threshold.

 Consider a 67-year-old, married, with $1.7 million in a traditional IRA. The urgency to convert to Roth rested on one date: the end of 2025, when the bracket structure was scheduled to return. The One Big Beautiful Bill kept that structure, and the IRS's 2026 adjustments reflect it instead of a reversion. For joint filers in tax year 2026, the 12% bracket runs to $100,800 of taxable income and the 22% bracket runs to $211,400. 
 Milkos / Getty Images The IRS's 2027 adjustments, released Nov. 05, 2026, keep the schedule: for joint filers, 12% runs to $104,050 and 22% to $218,250. That takes away the argument about a scheduled rate increase. Four arguments still stand: the years left before RMDs, RMDs pushing into higher brackets and Medicare surcharges, a surviving spouse filing single, and heirs inheriting pre-tax money. 
 Six Conversion Years Remain Before the First RMD 
 For someone born in 1959, the applicable age is 73 under 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(9)(C)(v)(I). The first RMD year is 2032, and the deadline for it is April 1, 2033. Each RMD is the prior Dec. 31 balance divided by the Uniform Lifetime Table divisor, which is 26.5 at age 73.

 A conversion counts as income in the year the money leaves the traditional IRA (IRS Publication 17), and it is permanent. Under 26 U.S.C. § 408A(d)(6)(B)(iii), a conversion cannot be recharacterized. The window for 2026 closes Dec. 31, and the broader window, those quiet years between the last paycheck and the first RMD, is the whole subject of our free Roth conversion guide.

 Social Security is not in the table. Benefits stack on top of the RMD, so $85,968 is the lowest taxable income this example hits at 73, and the divisor gets smaller every year after that. 
 Each Path Trades Tax Now Against Brackets and Premiums Later 
 Convert nothing. No tax now, and conversions can still start in any year through 2031. The projected pre-tax balance at the end of 2031 is $2,278,163. 
 Fill the 12% bracket. $71,470 over six years, with no dollar taxed above 12%. Conversion income stays below the $218,000 joint IRMAA threshold (2026 figures). 
 Fill the 22% bracket. $221,422 over six years. Each year's conversion lands in the first IRMAA tier: $81.20 a month for Part B plus $14.50 for Part D per person at 2026 rates. That comes to $1,148.40 a year for each enrollee. 
 The surcharge shows up later. Social Security uses the most recent federal tax return the IRS provides, measuring MAGI as adjusted gross income plus tax-exempt interest. A conversion done this year therefore raises the premium on a later year's notice. 
 Survivor Filing Single Pushes the Same RMD Into 22% 
 Under 2027 figures, a single filer's standard deduction is $16,600 and the 22% bracket starts above $52,025. For a single filer, the no-conversion RMD hits 22%. On a joint return, the same RMD stays in 12%. Under 2026 figures, the IRMAA threshold for single filers falls to $109,000. 
 Most non-spouse heirs must empty an inherited account within ten years, and that income is taxed at their rates. A Roth IRA has no RMDs while the owner is alive. 
 The decision comes down to three rates: the rate on RMDs plus Social Security after 73, the rate during the years one spouse files single, and the heirs' rate. The 12% fill costs less only if those later rates come in above 12%. The 22% fill needs later rates of 22% or more, plus the surcharge. 
 For your own return, check this year's projected taxable income against the 2026 bracket edge. Start from the taxable income figure on your 2025 Form 1040, then add the year-to-date distributions on your IRA custodian's statement before Dec. 31.
